title: Bernardo Arévalo, presidente de Guatemala: “Tenemos que oponernos a la normalización del autoritarismo y las dictaduras”
rawText:
Bernardo Arévalo, presidente de Guatemala: “Tenemos que oponernos a la normalización del autoritarismo y las dictaduras”
El único mandatario progresista en Centroamérica repasa los desafíos de su país y desgrana la actualidad política de la región durante su participación en la XXX Cumbre Iberoamericana de Madrid
Bernardo Arévalo (Montevideo, 68 años) ha tenido que remar a contracorriente desde que asumió el Gobierno de Guatemala en enero de 2024. Tras denunciar intentos de golpe de Estado para impedir su llegada al poder, el mandatario ha debido lidiar con el desgaste político, gobernar con una minoría en el Congreso, afrontar la suspensión y fragmentación de su partido y luchar para llevar a buen puerto una serie de nombramientos en instancias clave del Estado, como la Fiscalía General y el Tribunal Supremo Electoral. A todo eso se suman las turbulencias, las presiones y las responsabilidades propias del cargo. “Es complicado, pero no imposible”, afirma Arévalo sobre su día a día en la silla presidencial. De visita en Madrid en el marco de la XXX Cumbre Iberoamericana, el único presidente progresista de Centroamérica analiza en una entrevista con EL PAÍS la actualidad política de la región y hace balance a poco más de un año de concluir su mandato.
Pregunta. ¿Cómo definiría el estado de salud de la democracia en Guatemala?
Respuesta. Mucho mejor de cómo lo encontramos cuando yo tomé posesión. Antes teníamos una Fiscalía que estaba capturada por una élite político-criminal que extendía sus tentáculos a través de chantajes y todo tipo de cosas hacia el conjunto del sistema político. De hecho, mi victoria en las elecciones fue una recuperación del Ejecutivo, que estaba también en manos de esta red criminal.
Desde entonces, estamos en un proceso para luchar contra la corrupción y fortalecer las instituciones democráticas. Este año se daba una condición muy rara, muchas autoridades cambiaban de mando en un lapso de unos pocos meses. Al final, a pesar de todos los augurios negativos que había, lo hemos conseguido. La Fiscalía General se recuperó y tenemos ahora un fiscal que es un hombre de derecho y que sigue lo que establece la ley. Se ha elegido un nuevo Tribunal Supremo Electoral. Hemos hecho un cambio de contralor... La salud democrática de Guatemala está mucho mejor, pero la tarea no ha terminado.
P. Un 78% de los guatemaltecos desaprueba su gestión. ¿Le preocupa eso?
R. Mire, sí me preocupa en la medida que refleja un déficit de información y una prevalencia de redes de desinformación. Generalmente, lo que se dice “es que no se está haciendo nada”. Y ahí es donde nosotros estamos concentrados. Las inversiones que hemos venido haciendo en salud, educación, carreteras y política social está dando resultados y necesitamos que la gente vea que estamos invirtiendo en sus comunidades.
P. El regreso de Donald Trump a la Casa Blanca ha sido un desafío para el mundo entero. ¿Cómo gestiona las presiones de EE UU?
R. La relación con Estados Unidos se desarrolla sobre la base de intereses comunes. Los cambios de Administración generalmente lo que comportan son cambios de énfasis, matices… pero la agenda es una. La lucha contra el narcotráfico es para nosotros una tarea fundamental, porque es causa y a la vez efecto de la corrupción que penetra dentro del sistema político.
Hemos entendido que la migración es un problema de desarrollo y que necesitamos desarrollar las zonas más pobres del país para lograr contener esa hemorragia de seres humanos creativos y capaces que se van a buscar el futuro a otro país porque no lo encuentran en el nuestro. Al mismo tiempo, una vez que la Administración Trump definió una política para expulsar a inmigrantes, entendimos que teníamos que organizarnos para que su regreso fuera en condiciones dignas.
El tercer eje es el comercio y la inversión. Estados Unidos es nuestro principal socio comercial y la fuente principal de las inversiones extranjeras. Cuando la Administración Trump anunció cambios en la política comercial, nos preparamos y hemos tenido una negociación exitosa: alrededor del 75% de nuestros productos de exportación entran con arancel cero a Estados Unidos.
P. The New York Times publicó que habían acordado operaciones militares de Estados Unidos en territorio guatemalteco contra el narco. Su Gobierno lo negó. ¿Cuál es la línea roja en la cooperación en seguridad?
R. La línea roja es lo que establece nuestra Constitución. El establecimiento de bases militares, el paso de fuerzas militares o la operación de Fuerzas Armadas extranjeras en Guatemala requiere de la aprobación del Congreso de la República, lo que no ha tenido lugar. En ausencia de esa situación, lo que hemos firmado es una colaboración en la lucha contra los carteles de la droga, en cuanto a material y equipamiento, capacitación, inteligencia y acompañamiento para el diseño de operaciones de tipo táctico, es decir, presencia no armada. Lo que no existe en Guatemala, y ese es el error de The New York Times, son soldados norteamericanos involucrados en operaciones armadas porque legalmente no se puede.
P. Daniel Ortega afirmó que en Nicaragua no volverá a haber elecciones. ¿Qué puede hacer Centroamérica ante una dictadura en su propio vecindario?
R. En Centroamérica, y en general en América Latina y el mundo, tenemos que reafirmar el principio de la democracia y negarnos a la normalización del autoritarismo o inclusive de regímenes dictatoriales en nuestro entorno. Además, todos los países de la Organización de Estados Americanos (OEA) tenemos un compromiso fundamental con la democracia. Debemos retomar esos principios para orientar la política de nuestros países, pero también nuestras relaciones internacionales. En el caso de Nicaragua, lo que esperamos es que se den las condiciones para que haya un retorno lo más ágil posible a un sistema democrático.

title: "La derrota de Trump limita su poder interno, pero no necesariamente su influencia en el mundo"
rawText:
"La derrota de Trump limita su poder interno, pero no necesariamente su influencia en el mundo"
  - Autor, Jeremy Bowen
  - Título del autor, Editor internacional, BBC News
- Fecha de publicación
- Tiempo de lectura: 5 min
Donald Trump se caracteriza por usar superlativos, por lo que la magnitud de la derrota que le infligió una gran mayoría de los votantes estadounidenses el martes tiene un componente de karma político.
Pero no esperen que se retire dócilmente al ocaso de su carrera política. Perder ambas cámaras del Congreso estadounidense limita su capacidad para dictar normas, maniobrar y generar inestabilidad en su país.
En el extranjero probablemente sea diferente.
Como presidente de Estados Unidos y comandante en jefe de sus fuerzas armadas, conserva amplias competencias para utilizar el poderío militar estadounidense.
No es fácil predecir las acciones y los vaivenes de Donald Trump.
Como presidente, una de sus armas es el cambio de rumbo en sus políticas. Sin embargo, algunas cosas son constantes.
Una de ellas es su desprecio por aquellos a quienes considera perdedores, y su determinación de no ser visto nunca como tal.
El presidente podría verse tentado a usar acciones en el extranjero para encubrir la aplastante derrota electoral de las elecciones de medio mandato.
Podría intentar realizar maniobras que pueda presentar como decisivas y victoriosas de un presidente fuerte, sin que su victoria se vea empañada por unas elecciones que, insiste, a pesar de todas las pruebas, solo se perdieron porque su nombre no figuraba en la papeleta.
La guerra de Irán
En las semanas previas a las elecciones de medio mandato, el despliegue de las fuerzas estadounidenses y las declaraciones, a menudo beligerantes, del propio Trump intensificaron los rumores de que EE.UU. se estaba preparando para volver a la guerra con Irán.
En vísperas de los comicios, EE.UU. realizó un bombardeo limitado sobre una isla iraní en el golfo Pérsico.
Antes de ser hospitalizado tras sufrir un derrame cerebral hace unos días, el senador demócrata Chris Murphy asistió a una reunión informativa clasificada sobre posibles opciones militares para reanudar la guerra con Irán.
Sin entrar en detalles, Murphy condenó los planes calificándolos de "una locura" y advirtió que desencadenarían una "escalada devastadora".
Se ha especulado con la posibilidad de que el Departamento de Defensa de EE.UU. tenga planes para bombardear infraestructura civil.
Esto no solo constituiría un crimen de guerra, sino que además podría ser respondido con devastadores ataques iraníes contra objetivos equivalentes en aliados de EE.UU. en el Golfo.
Su lista de posibles objetivos podría comenzar con Emiratos Árabes Unidos, país tan cercano a Israel como a EE.UU.
Reacción iraní
El régimen de Teherán sigue de cerca los acontecimientos políticos en EE.UU.
No ha ocultado su satisfacción por el hecho de que las consecuencias de su bloqueo del estrecho de Ormuz se hayan convertido en un asunto político interno en EE.UU.
Teherán es consciente del daño a Trump y a los republicanos por el aumento sostenido de los precios de todo (desde la gasolina y el diésel hasta los fertilizantes agrícolas) por la guerra y sus ataques a los buques en el estrecho de Ormuz.
El presidente del Parlamento iraní, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, publicó una advertencia en redes sociales.
Dijo: "Por conciencia o por el precio de la vida, los estadounidenses dijeron NO A LA GUERRA, y respaldamos este mensaje. Si el gobierno de EE.UU. traiciona su voluntad pública para servir a quienes pagan y chantajistas internacionales, aprenderá que nuestro NO conlleva una pesadilla".
Benjamin Netanyahu, ahora primer ministro interino de Israel tras las elecciones de la semana pasada -quien se esfuerza por formar un nuevo gobierno- ha reiterado que quiere derrocar al régimen islámico de Teherán.
Según informes procedentes de Israel y EE.UU., está presionando a Trump para que vuelva a la guerra.
Netanyahu no tiene los escaños necesarios para formar un nuevo gobierno con su coalición saliente.
Pero si se reanudara y prolongara una guerra importante, y si los israelíes fueran atacados directamente, podría tener nuevas opciones para formar un gobierno de unidad que lideraría utilizando sus considerables habilidades políticas.
Guerra en Ucrania
El otro gran conflicto al que Trump podría prestar atención es el que existe entre Ucrania y Rusia, que ya se ha extendido más que la Primera Guerra Mundial.
Antes de las elecciones, levantó las sanciones contra Moscú para comprar diésel ruso.
Podría decidir prolongar y profundizar el alivio de las sanciones con la esperanza de mitigar de alguna manera la presión económica sobre los consumidores estadounidenses.
No se ha mostrado especialmente preocupado por la presión letal que sufren los civiles ucranianos, blanco de los misiles balísticos rusos, que ahora alcanzan su objetivo en mayor número porque las peticiones de Ucrania de más interceptores de fabricación estadounidense, financiados por aliados europeos, no han recibido la respuesta que Kyiv necesita y desea.
El portavoz del Kremlin dijo que Rusia espera que los resultados de las elecciones no afecten lo que denominó los "esfuerzos de paz" de Trump.
Donald Trump ha intentado sistemáticamente obligar al presidente de Ucrania, Volodymyr Zelensky, a hacer concesiones territoriales a Rusia para lograr un acuerdo que equivaldría a una capitulación para Kyiv.
Trump lo añadiría a su improbable lista de guerras resueltas y detenidas.
Después de la derrota electoral, Trump podría intentar redoblar la presión sobre Zelensky para que acepte las concesiones que ha rechazado repetidamente.
Se puede decir con seguridad que el presidente de EE.UU. seguirá erigiendo monumentos en honor a sí mismo en Washington DC.
Además, cabe reiterar que las predicciones sobre sus próximos pasos, tanto a nivel nacional como internacional, corren el riesgo de ser equivocadas.
Pero lo que sí es seguro es que no se quedará sentado en una mecedor

title: British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK
rawText:
A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.
“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”
The patient, whose identity is unknown, is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive in the UK on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred in a specialist ambulance to a “high consequence” infectious disease unit, according to an official document seen by Reuters.
A humanitarian organisation sent the worker to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.
The Royal Free hospital in London has a high-level isolation unit for infectious diseases such as Ebola; other centres are in Newcastle and Liverpool.
Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.
The current outbreak, declared on 15 May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases, and 5,000 deaths. It is the 17th in DR Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus, and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history. The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way.
Since the outbreak started, it has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last month Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus. She, along with a close contact, were evacuated to Switzerland for treatment.
In an interview with the Guardian last month, Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said the “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak meant it could reach the UK and other countries.
“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said. “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.
“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented.”
Other patients who have been medically evacuated for specialised care since the start of the outbreak include two sent to Germany and one to the Netherlands. Another case was reported in France in July.
British health authorities say the risk to the wider public from imported Ebola cases remains low and the NHS has procedures in place to manage suspected and confirmed infections.
There have only been four confirmed cases recorded in Britain since 1976, according to the UK Health Security Agency.

title: ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections
rawText:
The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.
The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls showed it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections.
In Kensington, a diverse Johannesburg suburb that has sustained repeated water and power outages in recent weeks, voters said they wanted to see change. The city is currently led by Dada Morero, the ANC mayor, in coalition with the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) and the rightwing populist Patriotic Alliance (PA).
“Service delivery is bad, it’s horrible,” said Tshepiso Makotse, 26, a call centre worker. “Water, electricity – everything, basically.”
Makotse said she had split her two votes, casting one for the centre-right Democratic Alliance (DA) local councillor and her party vote for the leftwing uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma. “I just want change,” she said.
Terrence Pieters, a retired boilermaker, said: “The infrastructure in Johannesburg is shot.” He declined to say which party he had voted for, other than it was “one of the offshoots of the DA”.
“I would like to see things get better and great people in charge,” said the 72-year-old. “But … there’s no one party that’s going to take over here. It’s going to be a circus, it’s going to be a coalition.”
Vote fragmentation means the ANC could still end up leading many city coalition governments while losing control of others.
Unstable coalitions are already a feature of many of South Africa’s 257 municipalities, and analysts point to their high turnover as a major reason for poor service delivery.
Johannesburg, a city of 4.8 million people that has faced water shortages for more than a week, has had 10 mayors in as many years. The neighbouring municipality of Ekurhuleni has had three mayors since 2021. To the north, in Tshwane, which contains the capital, Pretoria, the mayoralty has rotated between parties four times since 2020. In October, more than 800 people contracted a gastrointestinal illness from contaminated water in Bronkhorstspruit, in east Tshwane.
The ANC’s national leadership is open to working with the DA in Gauteng, according to South African media, mirroring the government of national unity, where the two parties are the largest in the national coalition. However, local ANC leaders are reportedly not in favour of a DA tie-up. Currently, the ANC governs in various coalitions across the province’s three metros, including under an ActionSA mayor in Tshwane.
In Johannesburg, the DA’s Helen Zille has led a spirited campaign, with viral stunts including the 75-year-old snorkelling in a pothole and kayaking along a flooded street. However, the former Cape Town mayor is still viewed with suspicion by many, especially black voters, due to past comments appearing to excuse colonialism. Some voters also point to soaring housing costs in Cape Town, which has been run by the DA since 2006, as a reason not to vote for Zille.
The former Johannesburg DA mayor Herman Mashaba, who now leads ActionSA, which is polling around 10%, has ruled out working with Zille in Johannesburg. Mashaba has called Zille a “racist”, an allegation she has always fervently denied. The ANC, for its part, has three possible mayoral candidates for the city, amid factional infighting.
In eThekwini metro, which contains the port city of Durban, the MK party was polling above 40%. Zuma, its 84-year-old leader, who has weathered and denied numerous corruption allegations, is set to take many of the votes of his former party, which won 42% in eThekwini in 2021 and is now polling around 10%.
The DA looks set to retain its majority in Cape Town, although probably with less than the 58% of the vote it won in 2021, as unaffordable housing turns more voters against the party.
South Africa’s electoral commission will have a week to announce the final results of Wednesday’s vote, which chooses councillors and parties, with mayors not directly elected. Parties will then have two weeks from the announcement to form councils and elect mayors.

title: Quiniela Nacional: resultado del sorteo de la Nocturna de hoy, lunes 02 de noviembre
rawText:
Ya se conocen los números ganadores del sorteo de la Nocturna de este lunes 02 de noviembre de la Quiniela de la Ciudad, la ex Quiniela Nacional. El primer lugar fue para el número 2875, seguido por el 1388 y el 3235, en segunda y tercera posición.
Los primeros diez puestos se completan con el 9113, el 4539, el 8418, el 1530, el 6595, el 9915 y el 0125.
El listado completo incluyó, desde el 11° al 20° premio, a los siguientes números: 2894, 6512, 4379, 5594, 5598, 2092, 4462, 5291, 1641, 1023.
A la cabeza quedó el número 75, que según el significado de los sueños representa al payaso.
Mientras que las letras sorteadas fueron: AUXY.
La Quiniela es el juego de azar más popular de la Argentina. Organizado por la Lotería de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires, la Quiniela no tiene pozo de premios, sino que se determinan en función de los aciertos, existiendo un tope de banca de 5 veces lo recaudado.
El juego de la Quiniela consiste en apostar una cierta cantidad de dinero a números de 1 cifra, 2 cifras, 3 cifras o 4 cifras.
¿Cómo se realiza el sorteo?
El sorteo de los números se realiza en las salas de la Lotería de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires y se utilizan cuatro bolilleros que van a conformar los distintos números, el primero corresponde al millar, el segundo a la centena, el tercero a la decena y el cuarto a la unidad, y cada uno de esos bolilleros tienen diez bolillas (esas bolillas tienen números desde el 0 al 9) y un quinto bolillero que va a conformar las distintas ubicaciones en el tablero (este tiene veinte bolillas que van desde el 1 al 20, que corresponden a las veinte posiciones en el tablero).
¿Cuántos sorteos hay por día?
Los sorteos se realizan cuatro veces al día: la Primera (a las 12 horas), la Matutina (a las 14.30 horas), la Vespertina (a las 17.30 horas) y la Nocturna (a las 21 horas).

title: Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientists
rawText:
It could be the opening of a Jurassic Park rip-off: scientists examining ancient dinosaur bones find what appear to be fossilised red blood cells, and traces of the molecule that gives the beast’s blood its distinctive crimson hue.
But that is what researchers are claiming to have discovered after analysing the hind leg bones of a small, meat-eating dinosaur called an Aratasaurus that lived and died in what is now north-eastern Brazil 115m years ago.
Electron microscope images of the dinosaur bones revealed small, round structures that resemble red blood cells in fine channels where blood vessels once ran, while chemical tests identified the presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around the body.
Such claims are controversial because biological tissues and molecules can break down fast, leaving little or no trace in ancient fossils. But if confirmed, it would open up entirely new avenues for scientists, allowing them to investigate dinosaur blood, metabolism and even their activity levels.
“We are seeing a mineral and molecular echo of the dinosaur’s original biology,” said Prof Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Western Australia who led the research team. “Fossilised red blood cells with distinct chemistry related to heme have never been found in situ in any fossil, let alone a dinosaur. This is a world first.”
The fossilised remnants of the Aratasaurus were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil, where researchers continue to study them. While analysing the dinosaur’s hind leg bones, Grice spotted the structures that resembled red blood cells.
The scientists’ suspicions that they were looking at red blood cells were bolstered when chemical tests came back positive for heme and its breakdown products. Tests also found traces of the amino acid building blocks for collagen, a key protein in connective and other tissues.
If the structures really are fossilised red blood cells, as the researchers contend, it raises the question of how they were preserved. According to Grice, a manganese compound called hausmannite, which formed in and around the blood cells, may have lent a helping hand by stabilising them prior to fossilisation. The same process might have helped preserve the amino acids, she added. The study appears in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
The work is already stoking debate. Prof Mary Schweitzer at North Carolina State University in the US, who has discovered remnants of blood vessels and soft tissues in dinosaur fossils, is not convinced Grice and her colleagues have found red blood cells. One reason for her doubt is that the dinosaur’s red blood cells should have a “nuclear bulge” making them appear dome-like on both sides. The structures Grice found are concave, suggesting they might be something else.
Schweitzer was more persuaded by the discovery of heme and collagen amino acids in the bone and said there was so much more to learn from exceptionally well-preserved fossils. Schweitzer added: “The conventional wisdom in palaeontology that all endogenous organics would disappear in a million years or less is being routinely challenged, and will continue to be as technological approaches to palaeontological specimens are more routinely applied.”
Another question the research raises is what other biological material might lurk in fossils collections around the world. On this, Grice urges extreme caution, adding that her work does not imply that large biological molecules such as proteins or DNA live on in ancient fossils. “Any extraordinary claim needs extraordinary analytical evidence,” she said. “The aim isn’t to find Jurassic Park DNA, it’s to determine how much genuine molecular information deep time can preserve.”
“The really exciting implication is that extraordinary molecular information may already be sitting in museum collections around the world, waiting for us to ask new questions of old fossils,” she added.

title: UK was ‘vehement’ slavery reparations should not be on Commonwealth summit agenda
rawText:
British officials reportedly insisted that discussions of reparations for slavery should not be on the agenda of the Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua and Barbuda – and even warned that Andy Burnham would not attend the meeting if the subject was formally included, according to a leading Caribbean political figure.
Ralph Gonsalves, a former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure in the reparatory justice movement Repair Campaign, welcomed Britain’s decision to enter structured dialogue on reparations, but said the UK had come “kicking and screaming” to the conversation.
Currently, slavery reparations is not on the official agenda of the Commonwealth Heads of Government (Chogm) summit, which begins on Sunday.
Trade, climate resilience and finance, sustainable debt, democracy and investment in opportunities for young people are among the stated priorities for the 56-nation bloc spanning Africa, Asia, the Caribbean and the Americas, the Pacific and Europe.
“My understanding from informed circles is that Britain was vehement not to have the matter on the agenda. The British officials – and in that regard they were joined by the Canadian officials – were even raising the prospect that if it is on the agenda the prime minister of Britain wouldn’t go,” Gonsalves told the Guardian.
“They also started to circulate this untruth that India didn’t want it on the agenda, but that was not so at all. India was very supportive at the UN general assembly resolution on March 25th, 2026. So they were spreading this false word about India.”
Gonsalves said that the relentless campaign by Caribbean nations, amplified by a growing regional and global reparations movement, has propelled reparatory justice to the heart of the political conversation at the meeting.
“Because of what happened at the UN, because of what happened in Africa, what happened in the Caribbean, and all the work which is taking place in Britain itself too, inside of the British parliament, inside of the British Labour party, both in the Commons and the House of Lords, it is an issue which you can’t duck any more,” he said.
He added: “The danger of not putting it formally on the agenda is what we see happening now, that everybody who could have foreseen, whether or not it’s formally on the agenda, even the nature of how the discussions take place at the Commonwealth, and certainly in the retreats, it would have been raised.”
Gonsalves said while the actual structured dialoguewas unlikely to happen at Chogm, it was expected that when the leaders met in their private retreat, the format and details of the dialogue would be discussed.
He said: “The British government, they’re coming, kicking and screaming to the table of structured dialogue. But at least they’re coming.”
An FCDO spokesperson said: “We categorically reject this completely untrue accusation. The UK has approached this conversation in good faith, and we have at no point told any other Chogm member what should not be on an agenda.
“Our position on reparations is clear but this government respects the right of others to raise matters as they wish.”
Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) Reparations Commission, had described the meeting as “the Chogm of reparations”, adding that reparatory justice was “the number one item” for the Caribbean as Commonwealth leaders gather in the region.
On Friday there was a historic shift in Britain’s position when the British prime minister went further than any of his predecessors by agreeing to structured dialogue and to consider an apology.
Though Caribbean governments and campaigners welcomed Burnham’s announcement, made in an op-ed for the Guardian, it was clear that agreeing on forms of reparations was still a priority for the region.
Guyana’s president, Irfaan Ali, welcomed Burnham’s statement and called for a Commonwealth subcommittee to work out the details of the dialogue over the next six to 12 months.
“I’m happy that finally the discourse has moved to a position where it should have been, where the British government is involved, because that’s the state we are dealing with,” he said.
Ali said the talks should move beyond attempting to put a price on the indignity of slavery and towards addressing its developmental consequences.
“How do we identify a system of support where the UK government, with its financial institutions, can sit with countries … and work on a development pathway, identify development gaps, whether in health, education, social services, infrastructure?”
Barbados’s prime minister, Mia Mottley, thanked Burnham for “breaking new ground”, while making clear that the two sides remained divided. “On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully,” she said.
Mottley identified an apology, investment in health and education, tackling systemic poverty and inequality, and fairer debt terms among areas where agreement could be reached.
The Bahamas prime minister, Philip Davis, said the talks were not simply about “historical remembrance” but “the enduring consequences of slavery and the importance of justice, acknowledgment and meaningful redress”.
As the meeting kicks off on Sunday, the 45th anniversary of Antigua and Barbuda’s independence from British colonial rule, King Charles is indicating he will not follow Burnham and offer a full apology, there is still a sense that the reparations fight is far from over.
King Charles and Burnham will be greeted with protests as they travel through Antigua’s capital, St John’s, to attend Chogm events.
On billboards, placards and T-shirts, in letters and at a candlelight vigil for the thousands of Africans trafficked to Antigua and Barbuda during the transatlantic slave trade, the message from the Caribbean will be clear: there will be calls for an apology and reparations.

title: Poll: Voters demand change and a check on Trump, fueling a steep Democratic midterm advantage
rawText:
Democrats have a sizable advantage in the battle for control of Congress days ahead of the midterm elections, a new national NBC News poll finds, with voters clamoring for change and voicing all-time high disapproval of President Donald Trump.
Registered voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, with Democrats leading Republicans 52%-45% — 2 points more than in last month’s poll. That includes a 21-point lead among independents.
Three percent of voters remained undecided as the poll was conducted from Oct. 28 to Oct. 30, and how they shift in the final days could tilt the outcome in dead-heat House and Senate races around the country. While the overall poll suggests that Democrats are poised to capitalize on a well of dissatisfaction with the president and his policies, there are findings that complicate the favorable picture.
When it comes to which party better handles key issues, voters give Republicans and Democrats about even marks, and the Democratic Party remains deeply unpopular. Meanwhile, Republican voters in GOP-held districts and in states Trump won in 2024 are sticking with their party — which is notable because much of the battle for control of both the House and Senate runs through this red terrain.
But there are also numerous signs of trouble for the GOP, with Trump at the center of a difficult political environment for Republicans and their slim majorities in both houses of Congress. The president’s disapproval rating has climbed to 60%, a new high mark in the NBC News poll across his two terms, and his approval rating stands at 40%.
After Trump won a second term in 2024 promising to bring down prices and restore the economic conditions of his first term, roughly 3 in 4 voters head into the midterms dissatisfied with the state of the economy. Nearly two-thirds of voters are calling for a change from the direction Trump has been leading the country, with 50% calling for “a great deal” of change, a new high mark in NBC News polling data.
And for the first time in 30 years of NBC News polling, more voters say they are dissatisfied with their financial situation (51%) than satisfied (49%).
“The Trump presidency can be summarized as the promise of two years ago and the peril of two days from now,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the survey with Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies.
Horwitt noted Trump returned to the White House after promising economic prosperity and peace. But now voters are expressing widespread concerns about the economy, with prices rising during the Iran war.
Amid those concerns, 64% of voters — including a third of Trump voters — say the president has fallen short of their expectations, with 34% saying he has lived up to them. Seventy percent of voters say the country is on the wrong track, a 9-point increase over the last year.
Voters continue to rank inflation and the cost of living as the most important issues facing the country, followed by government corruption, threats to democracy and immigration and border security.
“Democrats are in total control of the 2026 issue agenda,” said McInturff, the Republican pollster, noting that only voters who think immigration is a top issue are breaking for his party right now.
Democrats have a 1-point advantage on which party would better control inflation, a slight decline from September but still a warning sign for the GOP, which led on the issue in 2024. Republicans have a 2-point advantage on the economy, a marked decline from the party’s double-digit advantage on the issue in recent years.
Voters are also signaling that they are fired up about the midterms, with 70% ranking themselves as a “9” or “10” on a 10-point scale of interest in the election. Democrats have a 12-point advantage among those most-engaged voters, while Republicans have a 2-point edge among voters who are less interested in the election.
Self-described MAGA Republicans also say they’re significantly more interested in the election than Republicans who don’t identify with the MAGA wing, as Trump and his party push to turn out voters who typically sit out midterm elections.
That dynamic could be one reason why Republicans have leaned into culture war arguments in key races, attacking Democrats on transgender issues. The new poll shows a potential limitation of that strategy: Democrats have a 5-point advantage on the question of which party would better handle transgender issues, despite those Republican attacks.
It’s not all good news for Democrats, and the poll contains fresh signs that a number of voters are pushing back on the GOP, as opposed to falling in love with the Democratic Party, which remains deeply unpopular.
Just 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively, while 38% have positive views of the Republican Party. Around half of voters have negative views of both parties.
Still, some voters who are wary of Democrats are still planning to support them this year.
“Republicans have proven that they are not to be trusted. So I would rather see the balance of power shift, than maintain one party’s control,” one poll respondent from Texas, who voted for Trump in 2024 and is supporting Democrats for Congress this year, said in an expanded response.
“I don’t trust Republicans or Democrats, really,” the man added.
Republican disappointment
Frustrations among voters like that man from Texas, who backed Trump in 2024 and typically backs Republicans, are dragging down the president and GOP candidates this year.
Republicans are torn on whether the country is moving in the right direction (48%), or the wrong direction (43%). One year ago, Republicans said the country was going in the right direction, 75%-24%.
Now, a majority of Republicans (53%) are dissatisfied with the state of the economy. And 37% of Trump’s own party believe he’s fallen short of his promises.

title: As Midterms Near, Top Law Firms That Capitulated to Trump Are on the Sidelines
rawText: None of the firms that struck deals to avoid crippling executive orders are publicly involved in the major legal efforts to check the Trump administration’s attempts to meddle in the midterm elections, a review by The New York Times shows.

title: Obamacare Policies Hit Again With Steep Premium Increases for 2027
rawText: Premiums will increase an average 13 percent next year for millions of Americans, on top of an earlier steep increase. It adds to the problems facing the program, which the Trump administration has weakened.

title: This Device Uses A.I. and Lasers to Kill Mosquitoes
rawText: A Chinese start-up has developed a device that uses artificial intelligence and lasers to kill mosquitoes. But there are safety concerns for people and other creatures nearby when the device is in action.

title: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
rawText:
Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.
Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.
Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.
The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.
There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.
Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.
“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”
Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable.”
Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”
On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.
In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.
She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.
To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.
An informal security council poll earlier his month had placed the former Costa Rican vice-president Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.
At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”
He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”
Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.
“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”
Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed
